speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: asked the Minister for Trade and Industry how resilient is Singapore's economy and supply chain in the face of crises such as the COVID-19 outbreak.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: asked the Minister for Trade and Industry whether, as part of economic defence, the Government has considered nurturing a certain amount of domestic manufacturing capacity for critical necessities in product categories like medical disposables.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It has led to a sharp fall in tourist arrivals and a decline in domestic consumption, which have in turn badly affected our tourism, transport, retail and F&B sectors.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The disruption in economic activities in China is also expected to negatively affect export-oriented sectors such as manufacturing and wholesale trade.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The COVID-19 outbreak is a reminder of how unexpected external shocks can have a significant economic impact on us.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: To improve our resilience to such shocks, a key strategy that the Government pursues is economic diversification.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This entails the diversification of our economic structure, our markets and our supply sources.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: First, we have diversified our economic structure across different sectors.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For example, we kept the manufacturing sector at 20% of the economy and developed a range of clusters within the sector.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have also kept our services sector diversified, growing modern services like information and communications, alongside trade-related ones like wholesale trade.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Hence, even though the COVID-19 outbreak is expected to significantly affect the tourism and transport sectors, other sectors such as construction, and information and communications are projected to continue to grow and support our overall economy.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Second, we have diversified our export markets to enhance our resilience to market-specific shocks and downturns.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have expanded our network of free trade agreements to give our companies access to a wide range of markets.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In this way, we are plugged into growth markets, without being overly reliant on any single market for our exports.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Third, our economic agencies work closely with companies to diversify the sources of supply for materials, manpower and food.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Our companies’ supply chains have been put to the test in recent weeks due to disruptions in China’s industrial activity.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: While the impact varies from business to business, companies have indicated that they are generally able to cope with the disruptions because they have existing inventories or alternative suppliers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Most companies have also been able to manage the manpower disruptions arising from the travel restrictions and quarantine measures implemented in China and Singapore to contain the spread of the virus.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As for food supplies, we have not seen significant disruptions arising from the situation in China, due to our effort to buy from different sources over the years.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The Government also retains some domestic supply of critical necessities to mitigate any overseas supply disruptions.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Overall, our strategy of economic diversification has helped to enhance the resilience of our economy in times of crises, such as right now, during the current COVID-19 outbreak.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, even though for now, we are able to cope with the supplies such as groceries, but with the other countries also experiencing it, how will this affect our current supplies?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The second question is that in the longer term, we are looking at diversifying our economy, reducing our dependence on a single-source country – I would think that in this case, it is China – but for many of the products that may have many layers of processing, other countries are still highly dependent on this single-source country.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, as we diversify, how likely are we able to succeed in this endeavour, given that it also depends on the other countries and their responses as well?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That is the best way to deal with this situation.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We cannot quite control what is happening in other countries.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There is no global shortage of food supplies, for example.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The main thing is that for our situation domestically, we must also keep calm and do not have panic buying.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Because no matter how much you stockpile and how diversified your supply sources are, if there is panic buying, no amount of stockpile will be enough.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, that is one of the key things to be able to deal with this situation.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is to stay calm, buy what you need, but do not panic and there will be enough for everybody.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The second thing we need to do is to make sure that in certain critical areas, we are able to also advise people on the proper usage of the various supplies, for example, masks.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Otherwise, personal hygiene, especially hand hygiene, is still the most important.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Therefore, by doing this, you are able to prioritise the use of mask for healthcare workers, for patients, for frontline workers, the people who need it most.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is the best way to keep the whole community safe, collectively.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, that is what we have been doing in Singapore as well; consistent with the practices, as advised by WHO and by many of these other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Ms Tin's second question is about supply chain, and I think if I understand the Member correctly, she is saying that a lot of countries today are linked to certain supply sources like China.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, whether it is directly or indirectly, the supply chains are interconnected.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is definitely true because we are in a global economy, and no country can be totally isolated when it comes to its supply chains, its market.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But it is an issue of to what degree is your exposure.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Yes, it is a sizeable group, it is our largest group of tourists.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But we are, compared to some other countries, still better off because some of them have 50%, 60% or even higher.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I do not think it is possible to be completely delinked from any major economy in the current environment.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, definitely when something happens in one of the major economies – could be China, could be somebody else – there will definitely be an impact on Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But it is how we manage it by having a sufficiently diversified set of supply sources and markets, that will help us to be able to ride through these ups and downs in a more robust and resilient manner.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Could I ask him to answer Question No 5 again?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Oh, Mr Dennis Tan, would you like to follow-up?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Could I clarify with the Senior Minister of State, is the Government going to consider nurturing a certain amount of domestic manufacturing capacity for critical necessities in products like medical disposables?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think if Mr Dennis Tan had listened carefully, I did talk about the domestic production capacity for essential items and also stockpile.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I think that is ambitious plan, but given what has happened, my question to the Senior Minister of State is whether the Government should review this 30-30 plan, that maybe it should be a 30-25 plan, for example.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In fact, 30-30 is already very ambitious, but in the current COVID-19 situation, as it has borne out, I think the importance of building up some local supplies become even more critical.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, perhaps we should do a review and see in what way we could accelerate the bringing forward of the timeline.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And we certainly want to work towards that; not so much because we are focused on one number but it is really about resilience.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is really about having diversified sources of supplies, including local production.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But I think, Mr Seah being in the retail business would be very familiar, that it is not possible for us to be self-sufficient in many items.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, in addition to local production, which is one of the strategies, the other important strategy is to be able to diversify our import markets so that we are able to import from a wide range of countries, a wide range of different suppliers.
